events.title: TypeScript 5.0 released
events.summary: Microsoft shipped [TypeScript] 5.0 on March 20, 2023 with decorators, `const` type parameters, and multiple config file support.
events.about: [TypeScript] 5 aligned with ECMAScript decorators for frameworks like Angular and NestJS, and sped up the compiler for monorepos shipping millions of lines. It cemented [TypeScript] as the default for new JavaScript projects — frontends, backends, and infrastructure code.

narrative.whyChosen: [TypeScript] 5 standardized decorators and kept the compiler fast enough for huge repos.
narrative.whyImportant: Decorators unlocked cleaner framework APIs without experimental flags.
narrative.problemSolved: Large codebases needed faster builds and stable decorator support for Angular-style DI.

events.title: GPT-4 released
events.summary: OpenAI released GPT-4 on March 14, 2023 — a multimodal large language model powering ChatGPT Plus, Copilot integrations, and a wave of AI products.
events.about: GPT-4 improved reasoning, coding, and instruction-following over GPT-3.5 — and accepted image inputs in the [API]. It shifted AI from chat novelty to embedded feature in search, IDEs, office suites, and enterprise workflows within months.

narrative.whyChosen: GPT-4 was the capability jump that made LLMs credible for production coding and analysis.
narrative.whyImportant: Multimodal input and reliability gains triggered the 2023–2024 AI product explosion.
narrative.problemSolved: Earlier models hallucinated too often for high-stakes tasks; teams needed a stronger general model.

events.title: GPT-3.5 Turbo API released
events.summary: OpenAI released the GPT-3.5 Turbo [API] on March 1, 2023 — a faster, cheaper model that powered ChatGPT and thousands of production apps.
events.about: GPT-3.5 Turbo cut [API] costs dramatically while improving instruction-following over base GPT-3. It became the default model for early copilots, chatbots, and RAG pipelines before GPT-4 pricing dropped — democratizing LLM features in SaaS products.

narrative.whyChosen: GPT-3.5 Turbo made LLM APIs affordable enough for mainstream SaaS features.
narrative.whyImportant: Cost per token dropped enough that startups could ship AI features profitably.
narrative.problemSolved: GPT-4 was too expensive for high-volume chat; GPT-3 was too weak for production.

events.title: GHC 9.6 released
events.summary: The Glasgow [Haskell] Compiler 9.6.1 shipped on March 21, 2023 with improved error messages, OR patterns, and lifted language extensions.
events.about: [GHC] 9.6 polished the [Haskell] developer experience: clearer type errors, `MultiWayIf` improvements, and performance work for GHCi. It became the recommended compiler for new [Haskell] projects before [GHC] 9.8 followed.

narrative.whyChosen: [GHC] 9.6 improved error quality — a top pain point for [Haskell] adoption.
narrative.whyImportant: Better diagnostics lowered the barrier for teams evaluating [Haskell].
narrative.problemSolved: Cryptic [GHC] type errors frustrated newcomers and slowed refactors.

events.title: Cursor AI code editor released
events.summary: Anysphere publicly released Cursor on March 14, 2023 — an AI-first code editor built for pair-programming with large language models.
events.about: Cursor started as a Codemirror app, then forked VSCodium to reuse VS Code's editing stack while adding inline chat, codebase-aware completions, and multi-file edits. It kicked off the AI-native [IDE] wave — developers could ask questions about a repo, apply diffs, and run terminal commands from natural language.

narrative.whyChosen: Cursor proved developers would switch editors for deeply integrated AI, not just a chat sidebar.
narrative.whyImportant: It reframed the [IDE] as an agent workspace, not just a text editor with plugins.
narrative.problemSolved: Copilot-style completions were not enough; teams wanted whole-repo context and editable AI suggestions.

events.title: Silicon Valley Bank seized by regulators
events.summary: California regulators closed [Silicon Valley Bank] on March 10, 2023 — the second-largest bank failure in U.S. history and a shock to the startup ecosystem that held most of its deposits there.
events.about: Thousands of startups faced payroll crises until the FDIC, Treasury, and Fed guaranteed deposits. The run exposed how concentrated tech banking had become and pushed CFOs toward diversified treasury strategies — while venture funding was already tightening after the 2022 rate hikes and crypto collapse.

narrative.whyChosen: SVB's failure was the biggest banking crisis to hit Silicon Valley since 2008.
narrative.whyImportant: It forced startups to rethink cash management and sped up regulatory scrutiny of regional banks.
narrative.problemSolved: This was a liquidity crisis — startups needed immediate access to payroll deposits, not a software patch.
